subject: treasureHoard
pitch:
Category: Prop group.
Subject: treasure hoard: coins, gems, chest, crown, goblets.
Style: League of Legends.
reasoning:
I'm planning a treasure hoard module with coins, gems, a chest, crown, and goblets, aiming for that League of Legends style - stylized, hand-painted, chunky forms with rich saturated colors and glow, maybe hextech blue accents. I'm thinking through whether props need a root joint for the builder structure even though they're plain scenery objects.

I'll add a root joint called "base" and sketch out the overall composition: a chest at center-back spilling coins forward, a crown on top of the pile to one side, goblets on the other, and scattered glowing gems in varied colors throughout. I'm working out rough dimensions and coordinate placement, with the chest around 0.6m wide positioned slightly back, aiming for roughly 200 parts across the whole scene.

Now I'm working through the mechanics of the chest lid — setting up a hinge joint at the back top edge and figuring out the rotation math so the lid tilts open and back correctly using the right-hand rule around the x-axis.

Since the lid is a barrel-vault shape, I'm considering building it as an extrusion of a semicircular profile along the x-axis rather than a full lathe.

Building the arc points for a faceted lid shape, then planning to paint the wood with a grain texture for the planks. Now I'm sketching out the chest body as a box sized roughly 0.62 wide by 0.30 tall by 0.40 deep, positioning its base.

Rather than stacking the chest on the pile, I'll sit it on the floor with coins piled around it, with walls made of thin boxes plus a floor box, and an interior gold mound rising from the inside using a lathe or scaled sphere dome shaped elliptically to match the chest's rectangular footprint, peeking above the rim with a glow effect.

I'm planning to paint the mound with a scales texture in gold tones for a coin-like surface, then scatter individual tilted coin cylinders on top using a stick/scatter technique to add realistic detail without blowing the part budget.

Worried that coins near the pile could accidentally attach to the lid bone instead of root, which would make them rotate unexpectedly when the lid is posed later. I'm deciding to explicitly specify the root bone on all the non-lid geometry, so I'll build a small wrapper function that defaults to root for sticks, extrusions, lathes, and sweeps.

For the coin texture, I'm weighing cylinder UV mapping issues — the top cap disc would show the emblem fine, but the side would stretch the drawing ugly. I'm considering splitting the coin into a rim and a separate textured top disc to avoid that distortion, though that adds part complexity.

Actually that reeded-edge effect works nicely by accident. I'll keep the glow tint white for colored coins and flat shading per coin for simplicity.

For the ~45 hero coins I'll texture them via sticks, plus add 3 small stacks of 6-8 slightly offset cylinders for visual variety. For gems, I'm considering octahedrons or a custom lathe-based brilliant cut with crown and pavilion facets.

I'm defining a gem profile with the pavilion tip at the bottom, widest point partway up, and a flat table top, using 8 lathe segments to get that faceted flat-shaded look since anything under 12 segments shades flat. Assigning colors per gem type — ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz, and a glowing hextech cyan.

For the glow, I'm weighing strength: full emissive at 1 washes out the faceting since the color overrides lighting, so I'll use a lower strength like 0.4 for gems to preserve the facet shading while keeping the hextech core at full brightness. I'm confirming glow works fine on lathe parts since they still expose a mesh, and that flat colors give a single material per gem while paint colors won't support glow.

I'm also sketching in a few small sparkle accents near the gems — tiny billboard-style star cards, facing up and outward, double-sided, sized small (~0.08), with their flow oriented so they sit flush against the surface rather than tilting away.

Now I'm designing a crown for the pile: a tapered gold band with five spiked points, hextech-style glowing blue center gem, pearls on the tips, and a hint of red velvet dome inside, all sized small and tilted slightly as it sits atop the treasure.

Defining the crown lathe profile...

Still defining the point outline coordinates...

Using pearl color for the gems, then adding six radially-oriented jewels at the base of the tall band points, defining a gem lathe function parameterized by position, axis, size, and glow. Next I'm sketching the inner velvet cap dome visible from above the crown.

Adding the ermine fur trim at the bottom—a white lathe band painted with black spots to suggest tails—and planning the centerpiece: a large glowing cyan hextech gem on the front of the band set in a gold bezel.

For the goblets, I'm designing two: an upright gold one with a ruby band sitting atop the pile, and a tipped-over one spilling coins at the front-right, rotated on its side. Each needs a lathed profile with a hollow cup interior so the contents are visible inside the bowl.

Still refining the vessel's inner wall curve to keep it properly nested inside the outer profile...

Now I'm thinking about filling the goblet itself — maybe a glowing liquid disc near the rim, or a mound of gold coins and gems spilling over the edge for a tipped-over version, with a few gems poking out for the upright one.

I'm also placing a ring of small gems around the bowl at a fixed height, working out the radius based on the bowl's slope at that point, and considering a custom hand-painted gold texture with strong saturated highlights and shadows for a stylized LoL-esque look.

For the mound itself, I'll shape a flattened lathe dome to look like a coin pile, then paint it with a scales pattern in golds and ambers so it reads like stacked coins. I'll scatter a few extra flattened-sphere heaps around at different sizes with the same paint treatment to break up symmetry.

Now I'm working out the overall scene layout — positioning the main pile mound, placing a chest half-sunk behind it, and figuring coordinates so the composition reads naturally from the viewer's perspective.

I'm detailing the spilling gold ramp pouring from the chest down to the floor, the open lid tilted back, and the crown resting tilted on the heap at the front-left with its height setting the overall silhouette.

Now I'm placing upright and tipped goblets on the gold pile, with one spilling coins onto the floor, then arranging coin stacks of varying heights and scattering gems in multiple colors and sizes across the hoard, including a larger glowing crystal positioned above the gold as a focal centerpiece.

I'm working out the chest's construction details — wood planks with grain texture, gold corner brackets and straps wrapping the lid, a center lock plate with a keyhole gem, back hinges, a top rim band, and small foot and rivet details — and figuring out how to sweep the lid strap bands along an arched path to match the lid's curved profile.

Okay, so rx along world X gives the strap width while ry controls thickness along the normal, which resolves the orientation for the lid straps—I'll build the path as a catmull curve through nine points on the lid profile offset outward by 0.008, treating the lid as a single rigid mesh. For the body straps I'll just use simple protruding boxes on the front and sides rather than sweeps, finished in gold paint.

Now for the lock: I'm placing a shield-shaped gold hasp plate on the body front just below the hinge line, with a keyhole and ruby gem detail done via a small decal texture on a plane, plus a separate tongue piece attached to the lid that hangs down over the plate when closed and would swing up when opened.

I'm also planning an emblem for the chest — a hexagonal hextech-style crest with gold border, blue inner field, and a star, to use as a decal on the front plate and possibly echo on the coins. Sketching out the texture list: a coin texture with ridged rim and hex-star emblem, a sparkling gem texture, the hexagon chest emblem, and a combined lock plaque that merges the emblem motif with the keyhole.

I'm weighing a few more texture ideas — gold filigree scrollwork panels for the chest front between the straps (tinted via a grey drawing recolored by a color string), skipping separate velvet and pearl textures in favor of simple painted rings, and adding a sparkle card plus a glowing rune halo ring to sit behind the hextech crystal.

For the crystal glow, I'm figuring out placement: a radial cyan gradient disc plane with a hard-edged alpha cutoff, or better a rune-glyph ring texture glowing cyan, positioned standing just behind the crystal facing forward so it reads through the open chest lid, oriented and offset so it doesn't clash with the lid geometry.

I'm adding fur texture via paint spots for ermine trim, confirming the part count, and planning gem glow effects. I want an LoL-style bold, painterly look with chunky exaggerated proportions, so I'm making the crown oversized and thick.

Now I'm setting up the imports for the builder helpers, pulling in the paint, noise, and glow utilities needed for texturing.

I'm sizing the paint atlas for the treasure hoard builder, checking that a 1024px texture gives fine enough texel resolution for the pile's scale detail across the total painted surface area.

Now I'm setting up a root joint and small helper functions to simplify placing parts with consistent color and positioning, and thinking through how loosely to type the options object so it doesn't conflict with the builder's stricter typing.

I'm also writing a local coordinate frame class that converts an origin and Euler rotation into a reusable quaternion, so I can easily compute positions and directions relative to that frame...

Now I'm defining a gem-placement function that uses a lathe helper to build gem geometry at a given position and axis, scaling the profile by size and checking how the lathe's `at`/`axis` parameters accept vector inputs.

Working out how to position the gem so its pavilion tip sits embedded in the pile rather than floating on the surface, offsetting the origin back along the axis by a fraction of the gem's size. Refining the gem profile points to create a more faceted two-tier shape.

I'm thinking most gems should use a paint-based shading approach instead of glow, with brighter highlights on top-facing facets and darker sides to create a faceted look, reserving the glow effect for special items like the hextech crystal.

For a Hextech crystal I'm thinking of a tall hexagonal lathe shape with a lighter core and glowing cyan/pale tones, plus small tilted shards around the main crystal using slightly varied shades so flat glow colors still read with some facet variation.

Now I'm defining the color palette: golds, woods, blue accents, and gem colors for ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, and topaz.

Writing gold paint function...

Still writing pile paint logic...

Actually, I realize a full sphere centered at y=0 would sink its lower half well past the 2% height tolerance, so I should switch to using a hemisphere geometry instead, clipped to just the upper half so the mound sits properly on the floor.

I'm defining a set of overlapping hemisphere "heaps" with varying positions and radii to build up a lumpy pile shape, including a main mound, a sloped chest-front ramp, and smaller side lumps.

I'm testing different heap sizes and positions to avoid burying the chest too deeply — shrinking the main heap and shifting it forward still leaves the chest's front-bottom partially hidden, so I need to lower the heap's height further to keep the chest visible.

I decide to move the chest further back and resize the heap so roughly half the chest sits visible above the gold, which feels right for a hoard. I'm now reconsidering the chest's proportions, making it taller at 0.4 body height with a 0.17 lid arc, and adjusting width and depth to 0.7 by 0.42.

I'll keep the box body solid, with the gold hemisphere sitting at the top spanning nearly the full width so just a thin rim of the box shows, then add thin box pieces around the edge to form that rim lip.

Now for the chest's wood texture, I'm planning a paint function for the front face that creates horizontal plank lines every 0.1 units in y with darker seams, plus grain noise stretched along the x-axis by scaling the input coordinates before sampling noise. Writing wood paint function...

I'm thinking through how plank seams should orient differently for the lid's curved vault versus the body, deciding to parameterize the wood paint function by axis, then starting to lay out the chest body dimensions as a box.

Now I'm adding a base plinth and deciding to skip visible feet since they wouldn't show, then working out gold corner straps and vertical brackets at the chest's edges along with a horizontal band near the bottom.

For the lid, I'm computing an arched vault shape by generating points along a half-ellipse curve in the depth-height plane, defining the rounded profile that will be extruded across the chest's width.

I'm adding a thin velvet lining box to the lid's inner face, positioning it just below the hinge-side bottom plane so it moves with the lid when opened and sits flush against the body when closed.

Now I'm shaping the lid's decorative straps—curved arch sweeps running over the top plus flat end hoops near the sides, computing arc points with a slight radius offset for the metal thickness and translating them into position along the chest.

Adding more hardware details...

Still defining the hasp shape...

The plate overlaps the tongue fine, giving the look of a hanging lock. I'll draw the hex plane gold with a blue gem and keyhole at its center, sized roughly 0.13x0.15 with alpha cutting outside the hex shape, skipping a separate glow since it's not easily isolated. I'll also skip the front ornament panels since the space between the straps and center plate is too narrow to fit them well.

Instead I'm adding emblem shield decals to the side faces of the chest around x=±0.35 for visibility from an angle, keeping things simple otherwise. For the chest interior, I'll build a gold hemisphere mound with scattered coins and gems on its surface, plus a hexcrystal cluster with a rune ring plane positioned so it fits beneath the lid without clipping.

I'm deciding the saturated blue and gold hextech glow fits a League of Legends-style fantasy hoard aesthetic, so I'll keep it. Now I'm working out a heap-height function so I can properly place goblets and other objects on top of the uneven treasure piles.

Defining heap positions...

Since the back of the chest is bare at floor level, I should add rear heaps behind it too. Then I'll scatter coins across the heap surfaces, perturbing their normals slightly so each coin sits with varied orientation rather than all facing the same way.

Working out how tilted, half-buried coins should sink into the surface based on their own thickness versus a full embed, so leaning coins look partially submerged rather than floating...

Now I'm setting up the coin geometry as a short cylinder with a texture, making sure the UV mapping on the top cap correctly inscribes the drawing within the circular face.

I'll make the coin texture reusable so gold, silver, and copper variants can share one generator function with different color params, then sketch the hex emblem with a gradient fill inside the coin face.

Writing SVG code...

Finishing the diamond shape in the coin SVG, then checking that texture support exists on stick parts and estimating triangle/part counts to stay under the limit—coins at low-poly cylinders should keep things well within budget.

I'm reconsidering total part count: trimming coins down to around 120 to land within the 180-340 target range after adding gems, chest, crown, and goblets. For scattering coins across the heap surfaces, I need a filter to exclude points that would land inside the chest's hidden interior, since scatter only avoids other registered target meshes, not the chest body itself.

I'm also planning a separate coin and gem scatter for the gold spilling out of the chest, plus a stack-builder helper that places small coin cylinders in a vertical pile with randomized rotation and a slightly tilted top coin. Now I'm positioning the crown so it rests tilted on the heap, leaning into the pile with a rotated orientation so part of it appears buried in the coins.

Scaling the crown up so it reads as prominent against the wider hoard, then laying out its components -- the ermine fur ring, the gold band, and the pointed tips -- using a lathe profile for the fur trim.

Still shaping the lathe profile...

Adding pearl tips, smaller point outlines, and band gem placements, with the front gem as a larger glowing hextech stone in a gold bezel...

Then I'm adding a velvet cap as a scaled hemisphere sitting above the band, poking between the points like a cushioned crown top, keeping it simple without arches.

Checking that the dome radius stays within the band's inner radius confirms it fits snugly, so I'm painting the cap with a mottled crimson velvet texture and adding a tiny gold ball at the apex, then scaling the whole crown up to k=1.35 for proper proportions before moving on to defining a goblet-building function using lathe geometry along a vertical axis.

Still writing lathe profile...

Still working out the spilling goblet placement...

Adding a yaw of -40° so the goblet's mouth points toward +x,+z, then tilting the axis to -80° so the mouth lifts slightly, mimicking a tipped goblet resting on its rim and base edge.

Since the bowl radius is wider than the base, the bowl touches the ground while the base lifts slightly; I'll approximate the origin height as the heap height plus a small offset to account for sinking into the soft pile.

For the spilled coins, I'm placing them along the mouth's axis direction with increasing lateral spread and random tilt, resting flat at heap height, with gems scattered among them, keeping the front extent around z=0.95-1.0. For the goblets, I'm planning three: a gold upright one on the right, a gold tipped one in front-right spilling its contents, and a smaller silver goblet placed upright toward the back-left near another heap.

I'll mirror a left-back heap with a gem cluster featuring a large ruby, skip gold ingots for now, and plan out roughly 16 curated gems scattered around with varied tilt angles, leaning and half-embedded for a natural pile look.

For material treatment, I'll use regular gem shading for most stones to preserve facet contrast, but apply a flat emissive glow specifically to hextech crystals and the band bezel gem to make them stand out.

Writing gem paint function...

For sparkles I'm thinking of textured star planes with white-yellow gradients and cyan glow, placing about 8 near the gems and coin with varied sizes and orientation along a direction vector. I'll handle the texture and emissive glow through the material options, and note there's no paint needed for these plane elements or floor-level details.

For the crystal's rune ring, I'm designing an SVG with circles, ticks, and hex shapes in cyan stroke on a transparent background, sizing the stroke width to stay crisp at the target resolution, then placing it as a tilted plane at the crystal with full glow.

Tallying up the texture set now: coin gold, coin silver, sparkle, rune, lock, and emblem, possibly adding a filigree scroll texture for the chest's front panels with transparent background and gold tinted strokes.

Positioning two mirrored filigree panels on the chest front, figuring out the x-offsets so they sit between the straps and corner posts without overlapping the center lock plate, then sketching mirrored S-scroll curls as the design.

Writing SVG filigree scrolls...

Now I'm thinking through the dark wood backing plate so the gold scrollwork reads as engraved metal, and planning a separate hex emblem panel for the chest sides with a gold border and deep blue interior.

Setting up the module imports and builder scaffold for the treasure hoard asset...

Now I'm defining heap shapes as ellipsoid piles and computing a height function based on distance from each heap's center, then setting up hemisphere geometry for rendering them.

Flat facets at that scale may look too chunky rather than lumpy coins, so I'm considering displacing the geometry's vertices with deterministic noise to create a more organic, lumpy hemisphere shape.

I'll reduce amplitude slightly to around 0.06 so gems and coins don't float too noticeably despite the analytical heap height mismatch, since hidden faces from overlapping piles won't matter visually. Now I'm starting to write out the full implementation, aiming for roughly 650 lines, beginning with basic constants and vector helper functions.

Defining a gem lathe profile, then writing a helper function that builds a gem mesh along a given axis using that outline, sized relative to its girdle radius.

Rounding out the gem palette with topaz, aqua, and rose tones, then setting up a list of gem placements with position, type, and size data...

Now I'm mapping out where featured items like the crown and goblets sit so gems don't overlap with them.

For the tipped goblet, I'm calculating the mouth position and spill trajectory based on its yaw angle, checking whether it extends too far into the scene's depth and adjusting the rotation so the pour direction stays within bounds.

Now I'm placing the coin heaps and stacks: positioning one cluster to the front-left with varying stack heights, assigning gem placements elsewhere, and setting up a second goblet position for the silver piece.

Then I'm working through the full set of heap coordinates — A through I — adjusting each one's position, scale, and height so they sit naturally around the chest without overlapping, and now I'm figuring out where to place a possible extra heap J behind the chest, considering how close it can sit to the chest's back edge without clipping.

Now I'm tallying the overall bounding box of the whole hoard, checking the x-extent (roughly ±1.1), z-extent (-0.58 to 1.0), and total footprint (about 2.2m wide, 1.6m deep), comparing it against realistic proportions for a chest, goblet, and treasure pile to make sure the scale feels believable.

I'm placing the silver goblet at position H, orienting the chest's hinge correctly, and confirming the lid will open upward and backward without colliding with the crown or hoard pile in front. Writing the goblet lathe function...

Checking other points along the profile confirms the inner and outer walls don't cross, with the final segment from (0,0.215) closing back down to the base along the central axis.

The stem looks too thin after scaling, so I'm bumping its radius to 0.028 and adjusting the stem path coordinates accordingly, then double-checking clearance near the wall at (0.05,0.185). Now I'm setting up the cup's hemisphere interior, positioning it with appropriate scale and axis orientation.

I'm placing a band of six gems around the cup at y=0.205g, computing the wall radius there to tilt each gem's axis radially outward and upward.

Then I'm defining lathe profiles for a rim trim ring and a base trim ring, before starting on the knob gems.

I'll skip the knob gem ring and instead place a couple gems poking out of the filled contents alongside pile paint and coins, then move toward the tipped goblet with spilled coins and gems. Now I'm setting up the crown geometry, defining a scale factor and a new location with position and rotation values.

Writing crown geometry code...

I'm working out the band's outer radius profile to interpolate the gem position at y=0.055k, getting roughly 0.16k. I'm noticing the gems and the tall points share the same angular location, which risks a collision since the point's base is fairly thick near that height.

To fix the overlap, I'm repositioning the points to start higher up, around y=0.085k near the band's top rim, while keeping gems lower at y=0.05k so they sit clear of the point bases. That puts the tall outline's tip around 0.215k, and I'm now considering whether the smaller points should reuse the same angles or need their own placement.

I'm deciding to skip gems directly on the small points and instead add small studs or accent gems between them on the band, with bigger jeweled bezels at the tall point angles for a chunky, LoL-style jeweled crown look -- ruby and sapphire alternating around the band with a glowing cyan centerpiece gem at the front.

Now I'm writing the chest geometry code, defining its dimensions and position, then building the box mesh with wood paint applied via UV coordinates.

Adding gold dome coin pile, rim trim, and corner post geometry...

For the filigree panels flanking the lock plate, I'm sizing them to roughly 0.12 wide using the SVG's aspect ratio, stacking two per side vertically around the lock's center position.

I'm also planning the side-face emblems, placing them as planes attached to the left and right faces of the trunk, oriented outward along the x-axis with their height axis aligned to y, positioned using the trunk's width and depth constants.

For the lid, I'm laying out the hoop straps across the vault, positioning four of them along the x-axis with two inner hoops near the front straps and two outer hoops flush with the lid's end caps, considering whether to sweep these or build them as extruded arch end plates instead.

I'm also planning the remaining hardware: front/back lip bars, the hasp tongue, interior lining box, rivet spheres scattered along the straps, and hinge barrels, with the hinge sweep radius matching the arch geometry.

Writing sweep path points...

Good, the sweep offset confirms the inner face sits flush at the polygon vertex. Now I'm setting up the lid joint pose and making sure every lid part explicitly passes the lid bone, adding a helper to simplify that. I'm also planning a hextech crystal cluster in the chest, lathing a faceted crystal profile centered near the chest region.

Sizing out the main crystal shaft and four tilted shard crystals with glowing cyan-blue colors, plus a gold hex collar ring at the base and a rune-textured plane positioned behind the cluster for extra glow detail.

Working through the geometry so the rune ring sits behind the crystal without intersecting the rising lid, then adding sparkle planes near gem tips and defining gold paint variants—a base gold and a richer trim gold—plus an ermine spot pattern for fabric detailing.

I'm adding a velvet mottle texture for the chest lining and darkening the coin pile near the ground to fake ambient occlusion. Writing coin pile shader...

Writing coin-scattering logic...

Still defining exclusion zones and hit-based coin placement logic...

For coin scale variation and dome placement, I'm realizing I can use a general raycast helper that shoots down onto any surface to get accurate position and normal — this would work better than analytic height formulas for both dome gems and heap coins, giving more precise surface contact.

Writing SVG texture code...

Adding tick marks and glyph details, then checking pixel sizes scale cleanly at 512px before moving to the LOCK icon—designing a gold hexagonal shield with a keyhole, rivets, and gradient fills for the inner hex.

Now I'm defining color palettes and building the EMBLEM icon as a similar hex shape with a hextech sigil, gold chevrons, and a star, then setting up the filigree ornament and confirming all textures build once at the top. I'm also wiring up the glow() helper so it can wrap both plane-based and mesh-based parts with a configurable intensity, and typing it to accept anything with a mesh property.

I'm checking that glow() won't throw on flat-colored "paint" materials and confirming white base colors combine correctly with emissive textures. I'm also positioning spilled coins trailing from a tipped goblet's mouth, scattering them with random lateral offsets and rotations so they lie flat on the ground, and planning to scatter a few gems among them for visual interest.

Now I'm sketching helper types and classes for the build script, using loose typing to sidestep strict outline type imports, and setting up a quaternion-based Loc helper for positioning...

Building out the main build function...

The pole vertices all collapse to the same displacement value since y*3 is constant there, confirming consistency. With flat shading recomputing normals after displacement, I'm now setting up the heap pile parts by mapping over heap positions.

Rotating the yaw would skew the scaled ellipse axes and distort the lump shape, so I'll drop the rotation and instead vary each lump by seed/phase offset. Confirming the scale option accepts an array as documented, then moving on to double-check the lathe options signature, particularly the axis parameter.

Now I'm drafting a wood paint function that samples noise using stretched coordinates so grain features appear slow along the plank length and tight across its width, handling both horizontal and vertical plank orientations with a fractional plank-width coordinate for seams.

I'm computing seam darkening near plank edges, blending a base brown palette with noise, shading via a normal-based lighting term, and adding bottom-edge weathering, then moving on to writing the crown geometry code with specific location and rotation values.

Now I'm defining a lathe-based ring helper for the crown bands, using sharp corners to create crease lines, then setting up the ermine fur band profile with its distinctive notch shape before planning the ermine spot placement.

Adding gold trim bands and the velvet cap dome, working out the dimensions so the hemisphere cap sits properly on top with correct scale and positioning.

Defining the tall points shape with scaled coordinates and a sharp tip, then wrapping it in a paint instance for the gold outline.

I'm setting up the extrude call for each tall point spoke, positioning and orienting it radially around the center using sine/cosine offsets, and now I'm double-checking the cross product of the local axes to make sure the orientation is correct.

I'm placing a pearl at each spoke's tip using a small sphere, then adding the front gems around the band—six of them spaced 60 degrees apart with alternating colors (cyan, ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz), with the front gem getting a glow effect and a lathed bezel ring around it.

Now I'm working out positioning for the bezel ring and smaller accent gems placed at 30-degree offsets, checking that the radii stay consistent with the band's outer surface.

Good, that confirms the embed depth works. Setting rg=0.158k for a slight embed into the surface, then moving on to designing the hextech crystal cluster function using a tilted lathe profile.

Since a single-color lathe won't show facets naturally, I'll just accept the glow/emissive mix at strength 0.8 as a reasonable approximation rather than overengineering facet shading. Now I'm starting the sparkle placement list, positioning them at the crown's front gem, the ruby top, and above the hextech crystal.

Working through the hinge rotation math, the lid's front-top edge ends up landing around y=0.79, z=-0.75 after applying the -112° rotation to the local coordinates.

Doing the same transform for the vault top point gives roughly (y=0.52, z=-0.845), confirming the vault bulges backward with the lid's y-extent going up past 0.8. Now I'm checking the lid lining box position relative to the body, since after rotation it should form the inner red velvet face visible when the lid opens, though I need to verify the lining thickness is correctly placed below the lid's bottom plane.

Checking the lining span against the lid bottom confirms it extends slightly outward from the solid, so it stays visible when rotated open. I'm now tallying part counts across all elements—chest, crown, goblets, coins, gems, sparkles—landing around 330 total objects, and estimating triangle counts for the coin cylinders and lumpy hemispheres to make sure the scene stays reasonably light before writing the final code.

Writing stack helper function...

I want to avoid sharing a single coin geometry across instances in case the SDK bakes transforms into the geometry itself, so I'll generate a fresh cylinder per coin to be safe. For the dome, I'm placing a flattened hemisphere as the gold pile base and then scattering coins across its surface using the surface scatter utility with a minimum distance constraint.

Now I'm working out gem placement on the dome, positioning ruby, sapphire, emerald, topaz, and amethyst around a central crystal while checking distances to avoid overlap. I'm writing a helper that raycasts down onto the dome surface to find placement points and tilts gems slightly based on the surface normal.

Writing gem list data...

Checking x=-0.9 at z=0.1 fits within bounds comfortably, with low ry margin but still okay given the small height there. Adding one more gem at [0.95, 0.2, topaz], placed with modest height to stay safe near the edge.

Continuing to place gems across the remaining regions, checking each against the ellipse boundary equations: ruby, sapphire, emerald clustered on the left side, aqua and rose on the lower right, amethyst and another topaz upper right, and ruby again on the upper left, verifying each candidate position against its local radius constraints before accepting it.

I'm also setting up the small stacks of coins/items near the upper-left region and scattering extra small gems across the ground heaps for density. Then I'm positioning a tipped goblet, adjusting its base and mouth position based on yaw angle so it doesn't overlap a nearby gem, which means removing one conflicting gem placement.

Now I'm computing where coins spill from the goblet's mouth, adjusting the spill direction so it stays within the floor bounds near heap F, and checking the goblet's vertical placement so its bowl rests properly against the ground height at that location.

I'm now defining a silver variant of the metal paint function, reusing the gold version's structure but swapping in cool blue-tinted tones for the shadow, midtone, and highlight.

Chest metal parts will use a darker "antique" gold mix for the trim bands, keeping a brighter gold reserved for the crown to create contrast.

I'm now checking the plane placement logic for emblems on each side of the chest, making sure the orientation and "up" axis stay consistent so the artwork isn't mirrored when viewed from outside. Then I'll move to writing the complete implementation.

Reviewing the full builder API once more — lathe, extrude, sweep, part, stick, joint, pose, and frame — confirming parameters like bone, flat, and texture options are correctly supported, plus double-checking sphere geometry's theta/phi parameters for constructing a hemisphere shape.

I'm also verifying the rng helper's usage with cards and tileBox, and reminding myself to avoid unused TypeScript parameters by prefixing with underscores. Writing hexagon point generation code...

Still finalizing stroke widths, then checking the ordering issue where ground and heap variables need to be defined before they're referenced, plus making sure the lid's helper function is declared properly before use.
